title: My quest for peace and quiet
gist: Ioan Marc Jones argues that UK urban noise is worsening (46% of English households report noise problems), harms health and falls hardest on the poor, while weak, selectively enforced regulation has let a growing private 'quiet industry' (Quiet Mark, ANC headphones, silent appliances, calm car cabins) commodify calm for those who can afford it.

themes.theme: Scale of urban noise problem in the UK

insights.claim: The latest English Housing Survey found 46% of households report noise problems, with 42% of those saying noise affects their sleep; traffic was the most-cited source, followed by street noise.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: A large addressable base of noise-affected households underpins demand for soundproofing and quiet products.
insights.quote: 46 per cent of households report noise problems, with 42 per cent of those households claiming noise affects their sleep
insights.locator: Our homes are not much better.

insights.claim: Decibel Shield's city noise rankings put four of the world's 10 noisiest cities in India, many averaging above 80 decibels by day and 70 at night, while London ranks 40th, slightly quieter than Chicago and Paris.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Urban noise is a global health/quality-of-life externality concentrated in fast-growing Indian cities.
insights.locator: Excess noise is largely consigned to cities.

insights.claim: A 2023 Quiet Mark report found four-fifths of Brits value quiet time and nearly two-thirds crave a quieter home, while the CIEH found nearly a third believe their area grew louder in the past two years.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Rising perceived noise plus strong stated preference for quiet supports the growth of the quiet-products market.

insights.claim: Excessive noise exposure is linked, per Harvard Medicine, to memory impairment, learning delays, mental health problems and cardiovascular disease.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Noise as a public health cost could eventually drive regulation affecting transport, construction and data centres.

insights.claim: The CIEH found UK people earning under £20,000 were 10% more likely to report noise disturbance than those earning over £55,000; deprived London postcodes experience more noise, and council renters are more likely to have sleep disrupted than homeowners.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Noise inequality strengthens the case for regulation and makes quiet a premium attribute priced into housing.
insights.quote: Noise has long been a health issue and it has increasingly become a class issue, too.

insights.claim: The author argues that the privatisation of quiet largely serves the wealthy, while the poor face more noise and cannot afford protection, calling it 'a quiet injustice'.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Quiet as a luxury good: acoustic quality increasingly differentiates premium real estate and products.
insights.quote: The privatisation of peace and quiet largely serves the wealthy.

insights.claim: Sound subjectivity — people and cultures finding different sounds annoying — makes collective noise abatement hard because there is no agreement on acceptable levels and types.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Subjectivity explains weak enforcement; regulation likely to remain fragmented.
insights.quote: It’s hard to collectively police noise if we cannot agree on the levels and types of noise that we find annoying.

insights.claim: A 2021 study found Brits found railway noise less annoying than road noise while people in Japan had no such preference, and Taipei residents reacted more positively to insect sounds than Sheffield residents, who preferred church bells.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Cultural acoustic preferences matter for product design and urban planning across markets.
insights.locator: Different cultures have different responses to sound.

insights.claim: Conditions such as misophonia, hyperacusis and phonophobia sit at the extremes of sound subjectivity and make urban living especially challenging.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Niche but growing demand for assistive noise-management tech.
insights.locator: Some people have neurological and physiological conditions

insights.claim: UK noise law has evolved through the Noise Abatement Act 1960, the Environmental Protection Act 1990 and the Noise Act 1996, which established 11pm–7am night hours, but practical enforcement is limited by subjectivity and absent political will.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Weak enforcement means private solutions fill the gap rather than regulation.
insights.locator: Despite this, the UK government has a history

insights.claim: Noise from everyday tech and businesses — FaceTime on trains, boomboxes, the drone of data centres — faces imprecise or unenforceable regulation, which Will Dunn calls 'public nuisance capitalism'.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Data-centre noise is an emerging local planning/regulatory flashpoint to watch.
insights.quote: The less companies are regulated, the more they create the means for one person’s liberty as a consumer to impinge on someone else’s as a citizen.
insights.locator: Yet noise caused by neighbours is the most policeable

insights.claim: The author argues government reluctance to regulate externalities like noise stems from hard-to-measure harm, corporate disguise of harm, anti-red-tape politics, and tech lobbyists who now dwarf other groups.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Strong tech lobbying lowers odds of new noise rules affecting tech and data infrastructure.
insights.quote: tech lobbyists now dwarf pretty much every other group

insights.claim: The government uses noise as a pretext to regulate dissent: Section 63 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 targeted 'repetitive beats' at raves and the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 allows intervention against noisy protests, even single protesters.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
entities: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994
Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022
insights.so_what: Shows noise regulation can be enforced effectively when politically desired.

insights.claim: Large commercial festivals in Crystal Palace Park are tolerated despite annoying more people than illegal raves did, because their politics are mainstream, councils receive money and big business runs them.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Council revenue incentives favour licensed events over noise abatement.
insights.locator: But the act shows that noise regulation can work.

insights.claim: The market has stepped in to compensate for government failure on noise, creating a growing 'quiet industry' — the privatisation of peace and the commodification of calm.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for acoustic products, soundproofing, ANC headphones and quiet appliances.
insights.quote: It is the privatisation of peace and quiet, the commodification of calm.
insights.locator: After the kettle, I looked at other ways

insights.claim: Earplugs and noise-cancelling headphones are selling in higher numbers and at higher prices than ever, and a Quiet Mark survey indicates four-fifths of consumers consider product noise when purchasing.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Noise level is a mainstream purchase criterion; premium pricing power for quiet products.
insights.locator: The quiet industry is big and getting bigger.

insights.claim: Samuel Pye of residential developer Echlin reports a marked rise in 'quiet buying' across whole-home technology, with products chosen as much for acoustic discretion as performance.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Residential developers marketing acoustic quality as a premium feature.
insights.quote: We’ve seen a marked rise in ‘quiet buying’ across whole-home technology
insights.locator: The quiet industry is big and getting bigger.

insights.claim: Quiet Mark CEO Poppy Szkiler attributes rising demand for quiet to digital overload and macro instability increasing personal stressors.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Links consumer wellness spending to macro anxiety — demand may be resilient in downturns.
insights.quote: Digital overload and macro instability have caused a sustained increase of personal stressors
insights.locator: My washing machine features on Quiet Mark

insights.claim: Tech companies make anti-noise tech for noise tech companies create; Bose QuietComfort headphones cost close to £800 with adaptive noise cancelling, and second-hand AirPods cost £80.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: ANC headphone market benefits from urban noise; premium price points sustained.
insights.quote: Tech companies create anti-noise tech to deal with the noise made by tech companies.
insights.locator: The quiet industry extends outside the home

insights.claim: Car makers sell 'calm cabins', e.g. the Lexus LC combining a powerful engine/exhaust sound with a quiet cabin, letting drivers create noise for others while insulating themselves.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Cabin acoustics a premium-auto differentiator, a microcosm of quiet as luxury.
insights.locator: But the best example of the quiet industry

insights.claim: Quiet-certified products span silent kettles (around £200), quiet washing machines from Hisense, quiet robot lawnmowers and forklifts, and are seldom cheap.
insights.speaker: Ioan Marc Jones
insights.so_what: Quiet certification broadens across appliance categories, supporting premium-tier product lines.
insights.quote: quiet has become a coveted commodity
